newsitem.title: USA: US CREDIT OUTLOOK--Narrow ranges ahead of payrolls.
newsitem.headline: US CREDIT OUTLOOK--Narrow ranges ahead of payrolls.

text.p: Prices of U.S. Treasuries likely would remain in narrow ranges on Thursday as players awaited the nonfarm payrolls report on Friday, economists said.

Initial weekly jobless claims were slated for release at 0830 EDT/1230 GMT, but were not expected to have much impact ahead of the monthly number. The market could get support from the passing of a balanced budget. House and Senate leaders said they had pretty much ironed out final details on a balanced budget plan and could hold quick final votes on Thursday in the House and Senate.
The plan calls for a net $85 billion in tax cuts over the next five years, $115 billion in Medicare cuts over five years and a slower rate of growth for other government programs.
William Griggs, managing director at Griggs & Santow Inc, expected prices in the bond market would just list prior to the employment report. Few players were seen taking strong positions before then.

"The market's taken somewhat of a positive view going into this number," Griggs said. This was partially a reflection of the view that first quarter economic growth was unsustainable and significant slowing could be expected.
"If they couldn't make a case for firming in May, how are they going to do it (in July)," Griggs said. "The fear is they might have gotten behind the curve."

Griggs said average hourly earnings may have rose five or six cents an hour, versus market expectations of three or four cents. He saw payrolls rising by 275,000 in May, against market expectations of about a 225,000 increase.
In addition, Griggs said, there would have to be an adjustment to the high inventories level seen recently in light of decreasing demand.
Carol Stone, senior economist at Nomura Securities Inc, said initial jobless claims could fall slightly.

She said department store sales likely would decline as cold weather kept the sales of summer merchadise low. Stone saw no rapid acceleration in payrolls, but added that the Bureau of Labor Statistics seasonal revisions announced on Friday clouded the picture.
"There's a lot of uncertainty surrounding the number. We can't give a prior reading," Stone said.
She expected second quarter growth would show a pronounced slowdown from the first quarter.
Stone said retail sales next week would likely be higher than April, but not carry forward momentum.

"In late March we extended duration out of all bonds as the percentage of buyers was low," said Hugh Johnson, chairman and chief investment officer at First Albany Asset Management Co. First Albany has some $260 million under direct management and consults on another $1.6 billion for clients.
"I currently still believe we're in a period of noodling, or trendlessness," Johnson said. "We're headed for lower yields in the third quarter and most notably in the fourth," he said.
"The bond market is saying very clearly that the Fed will not raise interest rates at its July meeting. It shows up in the 91-day and other short-term interest rates," he said.
Investors bet heavily the Fed would not move in May and Johnson said it would be wise to side with investors rather than analysts as to the Fed's next move or lack of action.

The Fed's policy-making FOMC voted to tighten monetary policy by raising the federal funds rate by 25 basis points at its meeting on March 25. Under Chairman Alan Greenspan the Fed has not moved to tighten or ease only one time.
